title: DiskANN: when the index won't fit in RAM
summary: Co-locating each node's vector and adjacency list in one 4 KB page means one read per hop, and the beam width stops being a recall knob and becomes the queue depth: 100 reads is 10 ms serial and 1.25 ms at depth 8. The alpha pruning rule demonstrably densifies the graph, but I could not show its benefit at my scale.
html:
Phase 2 has given you two families and an uncomfortable choice. Graphs get the best recall per unit of work and demand random access, so they live in RAM. Cells and codes tolerate disk beautifully and give up some recall. Day 20 ended by saying the families split on whether your data fits in memory.

DiskANN refuses that. It is a graph, it runs from SSD, and the design is almost entirely a response to one constraint: every hop is a disk read.

The layout is the idea

Start with what a graph search actually needs at each step. It is standing on node c and wants two things: how far c is from the query, and who c's neighbours are. In an in-memory graph those live in different places and nobody cares.

On disk they must be the same place, so DiskANN stores each node's full vector and its adjacency list contiguously:

node record on SSD, R = 64:
  full vector        1536 B
  adjacency list      260 B
  ----------------------------
  total              1796 B      one 4 KB page, 2300 B spare

One read gives you the exact distance and the next hops together. The alternative, vectors in one file and edges in another, doubles your IOPS for no benefit. If you have ever co-located a row with its index entry to kill a second seek, this is the same move.

What stays in memory

The compressed codes from Days 21 and 22, nothing else:

1B vectors, PQ m=32

RAM:  codes 32 GB + ids 4 GB  =  36 GB
SSD:  node records            =  1.80 TB      50x more on disk than in memory

Search uses the in-RAM PQ distances to decide where to go next, which is cheap and approximate, and reads the SSD only to confirm. The codes are a navigation aid, not the answer. When a node is read, its exact vector is right there and the approximate score gets replaced by the real one.

So the rescoring stage from Day 21 is not a separate pass here. It happens continuously, as a side effect of walking.

The latency arithmetic, which decides the design

A search touching 100 nodes does 100 random 4 KB reads. At roughly 100 microseconds per NVMe read:

serial          10.00 ms
queue depth 4    2.50 ms
queue depth 8    1.25 ms
queue depth 16   0.62 ms

Issued one at a time, you are at ten milliseconds and the device is idle almost all of it. The entire difference between a usable system and an unusable one is whether you can keep several reads in flight.

Which is why DiskANN searches with a beam rather than a single pointer. The beam width is not primarily a recall knob here, the way efSearch was on Day 18. It is the queue depth. Expanding several frontier nodes at once means several outstanding reads, and the hardware does what it is built for instead of waiting.

That reframing is the thing to take from today. A design decision that looks like search quality is really I/O scheduling.

Vamana, and a measurement that did not cooperate

The graph is built by an algorithm called Vamana. Two differences from HNSW. It is a single layer, no hierarchy, which given my Day 19 result is less surprising than it sounds. And the pruning rule has a parameter:

HNSW:    drop candidate q if   d(p*, q) <= d(node, q)
Vamana:  drop candidate q if   alpha * d(p*, q) <= d(node, q)

With alpha = 1 these are the same rule. With alpha > 1 the condition is harder to satisfy, so fewer candidates get dropped. The stated goal is a denser, better connected graph with shorter paths, and shorter paths mean fewer disk reads.

I implemented it and measured. 2,350 vectors, R=32:

alpha   avg degree   recall@10 at search L=10   at L=20
  1.0         18.6                      0.957     0.991
  1.2         32.0                      0.963     0.995
  1.5         32.0                      0.901     0.992
  2.0         32.0                      0.872     0.989

The mechanism is clearly real: alpha=1.0 leaves the graph at degree 18.6, and any alpha above 1 fills all 32 slots. Fewer prunes, denser graph, exactly as the rule says.

The benefit did not show up. alpha=1.2 was marginally ahead, which is at least consistent with it being the usual recommended value, but 1.5 and 2.0 were clearly worse at constrained search width, and plain alpha=1.0 was competitive throughout.

I do not think this says much about DiskANN. It is the Day 19 situation again: a design aimed at a billion vectors, measured on two thousand, where paths are short regardless and no amount of extra connectivity can save reads that were never going to happen. What I can report is that the pruning rule does what it claims to the graph, and that I could not demonstrate the payoff at a scale three orders of magnitude below its target. Treat the alpha=1.2 default as received wisdom I have not independently confirmed.

The entry point stops being arbitrary

One small detail with an outsized effect on I/O. Vamana starts every search from the medoid, the vector closest to the centre of the dataset, computed once at build time.

HNSW could be casual about this because its upper layers exist precisely to get you somewhere sensible cheaply. With no hierarchy, the starting node is whatever you pick, and picking badly means extra hops spent travelling across the space before the search becomes useful. In memory those hops are nearly free. At 100 microseconds each they are the difference between a fast query and a slow one.

It is the same pattern as the layout decision. A choice that reads as a graph-theory nicety is being made on I/O grounds.

When this is the right answer

Roughly when vectors exceed RAM but the working set is not pathological. A billion vectors in 36 GB of memory and 1.8 TB of flash, at single digit milliseconds, is a single ordinary machine doing what used to need a cluster.

It is a worse answer than HNSW when everything fits in memory, because you have added disk latency to buy space you did not need. And it is sensitive to your storage actually behaving like NVMe: on a network block device with millisecond latencies the arithmetic above falls apart completely, and you want IVF-PQ's large sequential reads instead.

Today counted reads and assumed each one costs what the datasheet says. That assumption deserves more scrutiny than it usually gets. Tomorrow: SSD-native search and the I/O that actually dominates.
exercise:
1. Size your own node record. For your dimension and a degree of 64, compute vector bytes plus adjacency bytes and see whether it fits a 4 KB page. If it does not, you are paying two reads per hop and your latency doubles. Work out the largest R that still fits, because that is a real ceiling your graph has to live inside.

2. Do the queue depth arithmetic for your hardware. Take your SSD's actual random read latency, multiply by a hundred hops, then divide by queue depths of 1, 4, 8 and 16. Find the queue depth where you land inside your latency budget. That number is your minimum beam width, derived from storage rather than from recall.

3. Measure your device, do not trust the spec. Run fio with 4 KB random reads at queue depth 1 and at 16, and compare the measured latencies against the datasheet figure. The gap between those two numbers is the thing that decides whether this architecture works for you, and it is the input to tomorrow's lesson.
